{{Short description|Description of the ground state of a quantum system}}
The '''Gross–Pitaevskii equation''' ('''GPE''', named after [[Eugene P. Gross]]<ref>
{{cite journal
 |author=E. P. Gross
 |year=1961
 |title=Structure of a quantized vortex in boson systems
 |journal=Il Nuovo Cimento
 |volume=20 |issue=3 |pages=454–457
 |doi=10.1007/BF02731494 |bibcode=1961NCim...20..454G |s2cid=121538191
 |url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/343403
}}</ref> and [[Lev Pitaevskii|Lev Petrovich Pitaevskii]]<ref>{{cite journal |author=L. P. Pitaevskii |year=1961 |title=Vortex lines in an imperfect Bose gas |url=http://www.jetp.ras.ru/cgi-bin/e/index/r/40/2/p646?a=list |journal=Sov. Phys. JETP |volume=13 |issue=2 |pages=451–454}}</ref>) describes the ground state of a quantum system of identical [[boson]]s using the [[Hartree–Fock method|Hartree–Fock approximation]] and the [[pseudopotential]] interaction model.

A [[Bose–Einstein condensate]] (BEC) is a gas of [[bosons]] that are in the same [[quantum state]], and thus can be described by the same [[wavefunction]]. A free quantum particle is described by a single-particle [[Schrödinger equation]]. Interaction between particles in a real gas is taken into account by a pertinent many-body Schrödinger equation. In the Hartree–Fock approximation, the total [[wavefunction|wave-function]] <math>\Psi</math> of the system of <math>N</math> bosons is taken as a product of single-particle functions <math>\psi</math>:
<math display="block">
 \Psi(\mathbf{r}_1, \mathbf{r}_2, \dots, \mathbf{r}_N) = \psi(\mathbf{r}_1) \psi(\mathbf{r}_2) \dots \psi(\mathbf{r}_N),
</math>
where <math>\mathbf{r}_i</math> is the coordinate of the <math>i</math>-th boson. If the average spacing between the particles in a gas is greater than the [[scattering length]] (that is, in the so-called dilute limit), then one can approximate the true interaction potential that features in this equation by a [[pseudopotential]]. At sufficiently low temperature, where the [[De Broglie Wavelength|de Broglie wavelength]] is much longer than the range of boson–boson interaction,<ref name=":0" /> the scattering process can be well approximated by the ''s''-wave scattering (i.e. <math>\ell = 0</math> in the [[partial-wave analysis]], a.k.a. the [[Hard spheres|hard-sphere]] potential) term alone. In that case, the pseudopotential model Hamiltonian of the system can be written as
<math display="block">
 H = \sum_{i=1}^N \left(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \frac{\partial^2}{\partial\mathbf{r}_i^2} + V(\mathbf{r}_i)\right)
   + \sum_{i<j} \frac{4\pi\hbar^2 a_s}{m} \delta(\mathbf{r}_i - \mathbf{r}_j),
</math>
where <math>m</math> is the mass of the boson, <math>V</math> is the external potential, <math>a_s</math> is the boson–boson ''s''-wave scattering length, and <math>\delta(\mathbf{r})</math> is the [[Dirac delta-function]].

The [[Variational method (quantum mechanics)|variational method]] shows that if the single-particle wavefunction satisfies the following Gross–Pitaevskii equation
<math display="block">
 \left(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \frac{\partial^2}{\partial\mathbf{r}^2} + V(\mathbf{r}) + \frac{4\pi\hbar^2 a_s}{m} |\psi(\mathbf{r})|^2\right) \psi(\mathbf{r}) = \mu\psi(\mathbf{r}),
</math>
the total wave-function minimizes the expectation value of the model Hamiltonian under normalization condition <math display="inline">\int dV\, |\Psi|^2 = N.</math> Therefore, such single-particle wavefunction describes the ground state of the system.

GPE is a model equation for the ground-state single-particle [[wavefunction]] in a [[Bose–Einstein condensate]]. It is similar in form to the [[Ginzburg–Landau equation]] and is sometimes referred to as the [[nonlinear Schrödinger equation]].

The non-linearity of the Gross–Pitaevskii equation has its origin in the interaction between the particles: setting the coupling constant of interaction in the Gross–Pitaevskii equation to zero (see the following section) recovers the single-particle Schrödinger equation describing a particle inside a trapping potential.

The Gross–Pitaevskii equation is said to be limited to the weakly interacting regime. Nevertheless, it may also fail to reproduce interesting phenomena even within this regime.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lopes|first1=Raphael | last2=Eigen|first2=Christoph | last3=Navon|first3=Nir |last4=Clément|first4=David |last5=Smith|first5=Robert P.| last6=Hadzibabic|first6=Zoran| date=2017-11-07 |title=Quantum Depletion of a Homogeneous Bose-Einstein Condensate |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.119.190404 |journal=Physical Review Letters|language=en|volume=119 |issue=19|article-number=190404 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.119.190404 |pmid=29219529 |arxiv=1706.01867 |bibcode=2017PhRvL.119s0404L |s2cid=206302070 |issn=0031-9007}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal| last1=Chang|first1=R.| last2=Bouton|first2=Q.| last3=Cayla|first3=H.| last4=Qu|first4=C.| last5=Aspect|first5=A.| last6=Westbrook|first6=C. I.| last7=Clément|first7=D.| date=2016-12-02 |title=Momentum-Resolved Observation of Thermal and Quantum Depletion in a Bose Gas |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.117.235303 | journal=Physical Review Letters|language=en|volume=117 |issue=23 | article-number=235303 | doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.117.235303 |pmid=27982640 |arxiv=1608.04693 |bibcode=2016PhRvL.117w5303C |s2cid=10967623 |issn=0031-9007}}</ref> In order to study the BEC beyond that limit of weak interactions, one needs to implement the Lee-Huang-Yang (LHY) correction.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lee|first1=T. I. The General Solution and the Ground State|url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRev.130.1605 |journal=Physical Review|language=en |volume=130 |issue=4|pages=1605–1616 |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.130.1605 |bibcode=1963PhRv..130.1605L |issn=0031-899X|url-access=subscription}}</ref> or an extended equation, e.g. the Lieb-Liniger Gross–Pitaevskii equation<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kopyciński|first1=Jakub|last2=Łebek|first2=Maciej|last3=Marciniak|first3=Maciej|last4=Ołdziejewski|first4=Rafał|last5=Górecki|first5=Wojciech|last6=Pawłowski|first6=Krzysztof|date=2022-01-14|title=Beyond Gross-Pitaevskii equation for 1D gas: quasiparticles and solitons|journal=SciPost Physics|volume=12|issue=1|page=023|doi=10.21468/SciPostPhys.12.1.023|arxiv=2106.15289 |bibcode=2022ScPP...12...23K |s2cid=235670023 |issn=2542-4653 |doi-access=free }}</ref> (sometimes called modified<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Choi|first1=S.|last2=Dunjko|first2=V.|last3=Zhang|first3=Z. ==Form of equation==

The equation has the form of the [[Schrödinger equation]] with the addition of an interaction term.  The coupling constant <math>g</math> is proportional to the ''s''-wave scattering length <math>a_s</math> of two interacting bosons:
: <math>g = \frac{4\pi\hbar^2 a_s}{m},</math>
where <math>\hbar</math> is the reduced [[Planck constant]], and <math>m</math> is the mass of the boson. The [[energy density]] is
: <math>\mathcal{E} = \frac{\hbar^2}{2m} |\nabla\Psi(\mathbf{r})|^2 + V(\mathbf{r}) |\Psi(\mathbf{r})|^2 + \frac{1}{2} g |\Psi(\mathbf{r})|^4,</math>
where <math>\Psi</math> is the wavefunction, or order parameter, and <math>V</math> is the external potential (e.g. a harmonic trap). The time-independent Gross–Pitaevskii equation, for a conserved number of particles, is
: <math>\mu \Psi(\mathbf{r}) = \left(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \nabla^2 + V(\mathbf{r}) + g |\Psi(\mathbf{r})|^2\right) \Psi(\mathbf{r}),</math>
where <math>\mu</math> is the [[chemical potential]], which is found from the condition that the number of particles is related to the [[wavefunction]] by
: <math>N = \int |\Psi(\mathbf{r})|^2 \, d^3r.</math>

From the time-independent Gross–Pitaevskii equation, we can find the structure of a Bose–Einstein condensate in various external potentials (e.g. a harmonic trap).

The time-dependent Gross–Pitaevskii equation is
: <math>i\hbar\frac{\partial\Psi(\mathbf{r}, t)}{\partial t} = \left(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \nabla^2 + V(\mathbf{r}) + g |\Psi(\mathbf{r}, t)|^2\right) \Psi(\mathbf{r}, t).</math>

From this equation we can look at the dynamics of the Bose–Einstein condensate. It is used to find the collective modes of a trapped gas.

== Solutions ==

Since the Gross–Pitaevskii equation is a [[nonlinear]] [[partial differential equation]], exact solutions are hard to come by.  As a result, solutions have to be approximated via a myriad of techniques.

=== Exact solutions ===

==== Free particle ====
The simplest exact solution is the free-particle solution, with <math>V(\mathbf{r}) = 0</math>:
: <math>\Psi(\mathbf{r}) = \sqrt{\frac{N}{V}} e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}}.</math>

This solution is often called the Hartree solution. Although it does satisfy the Gross–Pitaevskii equation, it leaves a gap in the energy spectrum due to the interaction:
: <math>E(\mathbf{k}) = N \left[ \frac{\hbar^2 k^2}{2m} + g \frac{N}{2 V}\right].</math>

According to the [[Hugenholtz–Pines theorem]],<ref>
{{cite journal
 |author1=N. M. Hugenholtz
 |author-link1=Nicolaas Marinus Hugenholtz
 |author2=D. Pines
 |year=1959
 |title=Ground-state energy and excitation spectrum of a system of interacting bosons
 |journal=Physical Review
 |volume=116 |issue=3 |pages=489–506
 |bibcode=1959PhRv..116..489H
 |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.116.489
}}</ref> an interacting [[Bose gas]] does not exhibit an energy gap (in the case of repulsive interactions).

==== Soliton ====
A one-dimensional [[soliton]] can form in a Bose–Einstein condensate, and depending upon whether the interaction is attractive or repulsive, there is either a bright or dark soliton. Both solitons are local disturbances in a condensate with a uniform background density.

If the BEC is repulsive, so that <math>g > 0</math>, then a possible solution of the Gross–Pitaevskii equation is
: <math>\psi(x) = \psi_0 \tanh\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{2}\xi}\right),</math>
where <math>\psi_0</math> is the value of the condensate wavefunction at <math>\infty</math>, and <math>\xi = \hbar/\sqrt{2m n_0 g} </math> is the ''coherence length'' (a.k.a. the ''healing length'',<ref name=":0" /> see below). This solution represents the dark soliton, since there is a deficit of condensate in a space of nonzero density. The dark soliton is also a type of [[topological defect]], since <math>\psi</math> flips between positive and negative values across the origin, corresponding to a <math>\pi</math> phase shift.

For <math>g < 0</math> the solution is
: <math>\psi(x, t) = \psi(0) e^{-i\mu t/\hbar} \frac{1}{\cosh\left(\sqrt{2m|\mu|/\hbar^2}x\right)},</math>
where the chemical potential is <math>\mu = g |\psi(0)|^2/2</math>. This solution represents the bright soliton, since there is a concentration of condensate in a space of zero density.

=== Healing length ===
The healing length gives the minimum distance over which the [[Ginzburg–Landau theory|order parameter]] can heal, which describes how quickly the wave function of the BEC can adjust to changes in the potential. If the condensate density grows from 0 to n within a distance ξ, the healing length can calculated by equating the

quantum pressure and the interaction energy:<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dalfovo |first1=Franco |last2=Giorgini |first2=Stefano |last3=Pitaevskii |first3=Lev P. |last4=Stringari |first4=Sandro |author-link4=Sandro Stringari |date=1999-04-01 |title=Theory of Bose-Einstein condensation in trapped gases |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/RevModPhys.71.463 |journal=Reviews of Modern Physics |volume=71 |issue=3 |pages=463–512 |doi=10.1103/RevModPhys.71.463|arxiv=cond-mat/9806038 |bibcode=1999RvMP...71..463D |s2cid=55787701 }}</ref>
: <math>\frac{\hbar^2}{2m\xi^2} = gn \implies \xi=(8\pi n a_s)^{-1/2}</math>

The healing length must be much smaller than any [[length scale]] in the solution of the single-particle wavefunction. The healing length also determines the size of vortices that can form in a superfluid. It is the distance over which the wavefunction recovers from zero in the center of the vortex to the value in the bulk of the superfluid (hence the name "healing" length).

=== Variational solutions ===
In systems where an exact analytical solution may not be feasible, one can make a variational approximation. The basic idea is to make a variational [[ansatz]] for the wavefunction with free parameters, plug it into the free energy, and minimize the energy with respect to the free parameters.

=== Thomas–Fermi approximation ===

If the number of particles in a gas is very large, the interatomic interaction becomes large so that the kinetic energy term can be neglected in the Gross–Pitaevskii equation. This is called the [[Thomas–Fermi approximation]] and leads to the single-particle wavefunction
: <math>\psi(x, t) = \sqrt{\frac{\mu - V(x)}{Ng}}.</math>

And the density profile is
: <math>n(x, t) =\frac{\mu - V(x)}{g}.</math>

In a harmonic trap (where the potential energy is [[Quadratic formula|quadratic]] with respect to displacement from the center), this gives a density profile commonly referred to as the "inverted parabola" density profile.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Foot |first=C. J. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=kXYpAQAAMAAJ |title=Atomic physics |date=2005 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-850695-9 |pages=231–240 |language=en}}</ref>

=== Bogoliubov approximation ===

Bogoliubov treatment of the Gross–Pitaevskii equation is a method that finds the elementary excitations of a Bose–Einstein condensate. To that purpose, the condensate wavefunction is approximated by a sum of the equilibrium wavefunction <math>\psi_0 = \sqrt{n} e^{-i\mu t}</math> and a small perturbation <math>\delta\psi</math>:
: <math>\psi = \psi_0 + \delta\psi.</math>

Then this form is inserted in the time-dependent Gross–Pitaevskii equation and its [[complex conjugate]], and linearized to first order in <math>\delta\psi</math>:
: <math>i\hbar\frac{\partial\delta\psi}{\partial t} = -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \nabla^2 \delta\psi + V\delta\psi + g(2|\psi_0|^2\delta\psi + \psi_0^2\delta\psi^*),</math>
: <math>-i\hbar\frac{\partial\delta\psi^*}{\partial t} = -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \nabla^2 \delta\psi^* + V\delta\psi^* + g(2|\psi_0|^2\delta\psi^* + (\psi_0^*)^2\delta\psi).</math>

Assuming that
: <math>\delta\psi = e^{-i\mu t} \big(u(\boldsymbol{r}) e^{-i\omega t} - v^*(\boldsymbol{r}) e^{i\omega t}\big),</math>
one finds the following coupled differential equations for <math>u</math> and <math>v</math> by taking the <math>e^{\pm i\omega t}</math> parts as independent components:
: <math>\left(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \nabla^2 + V + 2gn - \hbar\mu - \hbar\omega\right) u - gnv = 0,</math>
: <math>\left(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \nabla^2 + V + 2gn - \hbar\mu + \hbar\omega\right) v - gnu = 0.</math>

For a homogeneous system, i.e. for <math>V(\boldsymbol{r}) = \text{const}</math>, one can get <math>V = \hbar\mu - gn</math> from the zeroth-order equation. Then we assume <math>u</math> and <math>v</math> to be plane waves of momentum <math>\boldsymbol{q}</math>, which leads to the energy spectrum
: <math>\hbar\omega = \epsilon_\boldsymbol{q} = \sqrt{\frac{\hbar^2|\boldsymbol{q}|^2}{2m} \left(\frac{\hbar^2|\boldsymbol{q}|^2}{2m} + 2gn\right)}.</math>

For large <math>\boldsymbol{q}</math>, the dispersion relation is quadratic in <math>\boldsymbol{q}</math>, as one would expect for usual non-interacting single-particle excitations. For small <math>\boldsymbol{q}</math>, the dispersion relation is linear:
: <math>\epsilon_\boldsymbol{q} = s \hbar q,</math>
with <math>s = \sqrt{ng/m}</math> being the speed of sound in the condensate, also known as [[second sound]]. The fact that <math>\epsilon_\boldsymbol{q}/(\hbar q) > s</math> shows, according to Landau's criterion, that the condensate is a superfluid, meaning that if an object is moved in the condensate at a velocity inferior to ''s'', it will not be energetically favorable to produce excitations, and the object will move without dissipation, which is a characteristic of a [[superfluid]]. Experiments have been done to prove this superfluidity of the condensate, using a tightly focused blue-detuned laser.<ref>
{{cite journal
 |author1=C. Raman
 |author2=M. Köhl
 |author3=R. Onofrio
 |author4=D. S. Durfee
 |author5=C. E. Kuklewicz
 |author6=Z. Hadzibabic
 |author7=W. Ketterle
 |year=1999
 |title=Evidence for a Critical Velocity in a Bose–Einstein Condensed Gas
 |journal=Phys. Rev. Lett.
 |volume=83 |issue=13 |page=2502
 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.83.2502 |arxiv=cond-mat/9909109
 |bibcode=1999PhRvL..83.2502R
 |s2cid=14070421
 }}
</ref> The same dispersion relation is found when the condensate is described from a microscopical approach to the [[weakly interacting Bose gas]] using the formalism of [[second quantization]].

=== Superfluid in rotating helical potential ===

[[Image:Quatro konical spring trapped ensemle okulov.jpg|thumb|right| Vortex dipole trap with topological charge <math>\ell = 2</math> loaded by ultracold ensemble]]
The optical potential well <math>V_\text{twist}(\mathbf{r}, t) = V_\text{twist}(z, r, \theta, t)</math> might be formed by two counterpropagating optical vortices with wavelengths <math>\lambda_\pm = 2 \pi c/\omega_\pm</math>, effective width <math>D</math> and topological charge <math>\ell</math>:
: <math>
 E_\pm(\mathbf{r}, t) \sim \exp\left(-\frac{r^2}{2 D^2}\right) r^{|\ell|} \exp(-i\omega_\pm t \pm ik_\pm z + i\ell \theta),
</math>
where <math>\delta\omega = (\omega_+ - \omega_-)</math>. In cylindrical coordinate system <math>(z, r, \theta)</math> the potential well have a remarkable  ''double-helix geometry'':<ref name="Okulov2008">
{{cite journal
 |author=A. Yu. Okulov
 |year=2008
 |title=Angular momentum of photons and phase conjugation
 |journal=J. Phys. B: At. Mol. Opt. Phys.
 |volume=41 |issue=10
 |article-number=101001
 |doi=10.1088/0953-4075/41/10/101001 |arxiv=0801.2675 |bibcode=2008JPhB...41j1001O|s2cid=13307937
}}
</ref>
: <math>
 V_\text{twist}(\mathbf{r}, t) \sim
 V_0 \exp\left(-\frac{r^2}{D^2}\right) r^{2|\ell|} \left(1 + \cos[\delta\omega t + (k_+ + k_-)z + 2\ell \theta]\right).
</math>
In a reference frame rotating with angular velocity <math>\Omega = \delta\omega / 2\ell</math>, time-dependent Gross–Pitaevskii equation with helical potential is<ref name="Okulov2012">
{{cite journal
 |author=A. Yu. Okulov
 |year=2012
 |title=Cold matter trapping via slowly rotating helical potential
 |journal=Phys. Lett. A
 |volume=376 |issue=4 |pages=650–655
 |doi=10.1016/j.physleta.2011.11.033 |arxiv=1005.4213 |bibcode=2012PhLA..376..650O|s2cid=119196009
}}
</ref>
: <math>
 i\hbar\frac{\partial\Psi(\mathbf{r}, t)}{\partial t} =
 \left(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \nabla^2 + V_\text{twist}(\mathbf{r}) + g |\Psi(\mathbf{r}, t)|^2 - \Omega \hat L \right) \Psi(\mathbf{r}, t),</math>
where <math>\hat L = -i\hbar \frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}</math> is the angular-momentum operator.
The solution for condensate wavefunction <math>\Psi(\mathbf{r}, t)</math> is a superposition of two phase-conjugated matter–wave vortices:
: <math>
 \Psi(\mathbf{r}, t) \sim \exp\left(-\frac{r^2}{2D^2}\right) r^{|\ell|} \times
  \big(\exp(-i\omega_+ t + ik_+ z + i\ell \theta) + \exp(-i\omega_- t - ik_- z - i\ell \theta) \big).
</math>
<!-- Deleted image removed: [[Image:BEC loaded in double helix trap wikipedia.jpg|thumb|right|350px|Atomic cloud trapped by rotating helical potential.]] -->
The macroscopically observable momentum of condensate is
: <math>\langle \Psi | \hat P | \Psi \rangle = N_\text{at} \hbar (k_+ - k_-),</math>
where <math>N_\text{at}</math> is number of atoms in condensate. 
This means that atomic ensemble moves coherently along <math>z</math> axis with [[group velocity]] whose direction is defined by signs of topological charge <math>\ell</math> and angular velocity <math>\Omega</math>:<ref name="Okulov2013">
{{cite journal
 |author=A. Yu. Okulov
 |year=2013
 |title=Superfluid rotation sensor with helical laser trap
 |journal=J. Low Temp. Phys.
 |volume=171 |issue=3 |pages=397–407
 |doi=10.1007/s10909-012-0837-7 |arxiv=1207.3537 |bibcode=2013JLTP..171..397O|s2cid=118601627
}}
</ref>
: <math>V_z = \frac{2\Omega \ell}{k_+ + k_-}.</math>

The angular momentum  of helically trapped condensate is exactly zero:<ref name="Okulov2012"/>
: <math>\langle \Psi | \hat L | \Psi \rangle = N_\text{at} [\ell\hbar - \ell\hbar] = 0.</math>

Numerical modeling of cold atomic ensemble in spiral potential have shown the confinement of individual atomic trajectories within helical potential well.<ref name="Lembessis2016">
{{cite journal
 |author=A. Al. Rsheed1, A. Lyras, V. E. Lembessis, O. M. Aldossary
 |year=2016
 |title=Guiding of atoms in helical optical potential structures
 |journal=J. Phys. B: At. Mol. Opt. Phys.
 |volume=49 |issue=12 |article-number= 125002
 |doi=10.1088/0953-4075/49/12/125002 |bibcode=2016JPhB...49l5002R
 |s2cid=124660886
}}</ref>

== Derivations and generalisations ==
The Gross–Pitaevskii equation can also be derived as the semi-classical limit of the many body theory of s-wave interacting identical bosons represented in terms of coherent states.<ref name="Steel1998">{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1103/PhysRevA.58.4824| volume = 58| issue = 6| pages = 4824–4835| last1 = Steel| first1 = M J| last2 = Olsen| first2 = M K| last3 = Plimak| first3 = L I| last4 = Drummond| first4 = P D| last5 = Tan| first5 = S M| last6 = Collett| first6 = M J| last7 = Walls| first7 = D F| last8 = Graham| first8 = R| title = Dynamical quantum noise in trapped Bose-Einstein condensates| journal = Physical Review A| date = 1998| arxiv = cond-mat/9807349| bibcode = 1998PhRvA..58.4824S| s2cid = 43217083}}</ref> The semi-classical limit is reached for a large number of quanta, expressing the field theory either in the positive-P representation (generalised [[Glauber–Sudarshan P representation|Glauber-Sudarshan P representation]]) or [[Wigner quasiprobability distribution|Wigner representation]]. 
 
Finite-temperature effects can be treated within a generalised Gross–Pitaevskii equation by including scattering between condensate and noncondensate atoms,<ref>{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1023/A:1021846002995| volume = 116| issue = 3–4| pages = 277–345| last1 = Zaremba| first1 = E| last2 = Nikuni| first2 = T| last3 = Griffin| first3 = A| title = Dynamics of Trapped Bose Gases at Finite Temperatures| journal = Journal of Low Temperature Physics| date = 1999| s2cid = 37753}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1023/A:1021897703053| volume = 114| issue = 1–2| pages = 11–108| last = Stoof| first = H T C| title = Coherent versus incoherent dynamics during Bose-Einstein condensation in atomic gases| journal = Journal of Low Temperature Physics| date = 1999| s2cid = 16107086}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1103/PhysRevLett.87.160402| volume = 87| issue = 16| article-number = 160402| last1 = Davis| first1 = M J| last2 = Morgan| first2 = S A| last3 = Burnett| == External links ==
* [https://trotter-suzuki-mpi.github.io/ Trotter-Suzuki-MPI] Trotter-Suzuki-MPI is a library for large-scale simulations based on the [[Lie product formula|Trotter-Suzuki decomposition]] that can also address the Gross–Pitaevskii equation.
* [http://www.xmds.org/ XMDS] XMDS is a spectral partial differential equation library that can be used to solve the Gross–Pitaevskii equation.
